claims.text: The baseline is a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy containing no tungsten.
Each constituent element in the baseline alloy is intended to be present within 5–35 at%.
The intervention is incorporation of 2–5 at% tungsten during melting and processing.
Adding 2–5 at% tungsten will improve the alloy's elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the tungsten-free baseline.
Tungsten addition will produce tungsten-enriched precipitates.
Tungsten addition will refine the grain structure, especially at grain boundaries.
Tungsten has a high melting point.
Tungsten has limited solubility in the proposed titanium- and nickel-primary alloy.
Tungsten's high melting point and limited solubility will promote secondary-phase formation.
The tungsten-induced secondary phases will pin grain boundaries.
The tungsten-induced secondary phases will impede dislocation motion.
Grain-boundary pinning and impeded dislocation motion will reduce creep and high-temperature softening.
The tungsten-doped alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength than the baseline.
The tungsten-doped alloy will have lower high-temperature creep strain than the baseline.
The expected improvement is approximately 15–20% relative to the baseline.
The proposed effect is bounded to 2–5 at% tungsten and testing temperatures of 700–1000°C.

contradictions.description: The stated high-entropy-alloy definition requires constituent elements to be present at 5–35 at%, but the intervention permits tungsten contents as low as 2 at%. Thus part of the proposed range violates the stated compositional definition if tungsten is counted as a constituent element.

The predicted improvement is 15–20%, whereas the falsification rule accepts a 10–15% yield-strength increase, or merely a statistically significant creep-strain reduction, as sufficient to avoid falsification. The decisive criterion therefore does not directly test the full quantitative prediction.
